article.title: Artificial artists

items.sentence_raw: The Painting Fool is one of a growing number of computer programs which, so their makers claim, possess creative talents.
items.explain: Q27: The first paragraph lists big successes: *'Classical music... had audiences enraptured'*, *'Artworks... sold for thousands'*, and *'software... creates art that could not have been imagined'*. All these examples show that **a great deal of progress** has already happened. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Classical music by an artificial composer has had audiences enraptured, and even tricked them into believing a human was behind the score.
items.explain: Q27: The first paragraph lists big successes: *'Classical music... had audiences enraptured'*, *'Artworks... sold for thousands'*, and *'software... creates art that could not have been imagined'*. All these examples show that **a great deal of progress** has already happened. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Artworks painted by a robot have sold for thousands of dollars and been hung in prestigious galleries.
items.explain: Q27: The first paragraph lists big successes: *'Classical music... had audiences enraptured'*, *'Artworks... sold for thousands'*, and *'software... creates art that could not have been imagined'*. All these examples show that **a great deal of progress** has already happened. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: And software has been built which creates art that could not have been imagined by the programmer.
Human beings are the only species to perform sophisticated creative acts regularly.
If we can break this process down into computer code, where does that leave human creativity?
"This is a question at the very core of humanity," says Geraint Wiggins, a computational creativity researcher at Goldsmiths, University of London.
"It scares a lot of people.
They are worried that it is taking something special away from what it means to be human."
items.explain: Q28: Wiggins says people are scared because *'it is taking something special away from what it means to be human'*. **'Something special'** about being human is a **fundamental human quality** — like creativity. So the worry is that computer art **undermines** this quality, making the answer **C**.

items.sentence_raw: To some extent, we are all familiar with computerised art.
The question is: where does the work of the artist stop and the creativity of the computer begin?
Consider one of the oldest machine artists, Aaron, a robot that has had paintings exhibited in London's Tate Modern and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art.
Aaron can pick up a paintbrush and paint on canvas on its own.
Impressive perhaps, but it is still little more than a tool to realise the programmer's own creative ideas.
Simon Colton, the designer of the Painting Fool, is keen to make sure his creation doesn't attract the same criticism.
Unlike earlier 'artists' such as Aaron, the Painting Fool only needs minimal direction and can come up with its own concepts by going online for material.
items.explain: Q29: The key difference is about where ideas come from. The passage says *'Unlike earlier 'artists' such as Aaron, the Painting Fool... can come up with its own concepts by going online for material'*. So Aaron depends on the programmer, but the Painting Fool finds its own **source of subject matter**. The answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: The software runs its own web searches and trawls through social media sites.
It is now beginning to display a kind of imagination too, creating pictures from scratch.
One of its original works is a series of fuzzy landscapes, depicting trees and sky.
While some might say they have a mechanical look, Colton argues that such reactions arise from people's double standards towards software-produced and human-produced art.
items.explain: Q30: Colton argues that negative reactions *'arise from people's double standards towards software-produced and human-produced art'*. **'Double standards'** means judging by **different criteria** — being stricter with computers than with humans. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: After all, he says, consider that the Painting Fool painted the landscapes without referring to a photo.
"If a child painted a new scene from its head, you'd say it has a certain level of imagination," he points out.
"The same should be true of a machine."
Software bugs can also lead to unexpected results.
Some of the Painting Fool's paintings of a chair came out in black and white, thanks to a technical glitch.
This gives the work an eerie, ghostlike quality.
items.explain: Q31: The chair paintings resulted from a *'technical glitch'*, but the passage says *'This gives the work an eerie, ghostlike quality'*. **'Eerie, ghostlike'** is a **particularly striking effect**, not a failure. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Human artists like the renowned Ellsworth Kelly are lauded for limiting their colour palette - so why should computers be any different?
Researchers like Colton don't believe it is right to measure machine creativity directly to that of humans who 'have had millennia to develop our skills'.
items.explain: Q32: Colton says it is not right to measure machine creativity directly to humans who *'have had millennia to develop our skills'*. This means we should avoid **comparing** human and computer artistic achievements right now. So the correct ending is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: Others, though, are fascinated by the prospect that a computer might create something as original and subtle as our best artists.
So far, only one has come close.
Composer David Cope invented a program called Experiments in Musical Intelligence, or EMI.
Not only did EMI create compositions in Cope's style, but also that of the most revered classical composers, including Bach, Chopin and Mozart.
items.explain: Q33: EMI *'fooled classical music experts into thinking they were hearing genuine Bach'*. **'Fooled'** means the music was **virtually indistinguishable** from a human's work. So the correct ending is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Audiences were moved to tears, and EMI even fooled classical music experts into thinking they were hearing genuine Bach.
items.explain: Q33: EMI *'fooled classical music experts into thinking they were hearing genuine Bach'*. **'Fooled'** means the music was **virtually indistinguishable** from a human's work. So the correct ending is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Not everyone was impressed however.
Some, such as Wiggins, have blasted Cope's work as pseudoscience, and condemned him for his deliberately vague explanation of how the software worked.
items.explain: Q34: Wiggins *'condemned him for his deliberately vague explanation of how the software worked'*. A **'vague explanation'** means he was **not revealing the technical details**. So the correct ending is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: Meanwhile, Douglas Hofstadter of Indiana University said EMI created replicas which still rely completely on the original artist's creative impulses.
items.explain: Q35: Hofstadter said EMI created *'replicas which still rely completely on the original artist's creative impulses'*. This means the work was **entirely dependent on the imagination of its creator**, not the computer's. So the correct ending is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: When audiences found out the truth they were often outraged with Cope, and one music lover even tried to punch him.
items.explain: Q36: The passage says *'When audiences found out the truth they were often outraged'*. **'Found out the truth'** means **discovering it was the product of a computer program**. So the correct ending is **G**.

items.sentence_raw: Amid such controversy, Cope destroyed EMI's vital databases.
But why did so many people love the music, yet recoil when they discovered how it was composed?
items.explain: Q38: The passage asks why people *'recoil when they discovered how it was composed'*, then says Moffat's study *'provides a clue'*. A **'clue'** means it helps **explain** the reaction. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: A study by computer scientist David Moffat of Glasgow Caledonian University provides a clue.
items.explain: Q38: The passage asks why people *'recoil when they discovered how it was composed'*, then says Moffat's study *'provides a clue'*. A **'clue'** means it helps **explain** the reaction. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: He asked both expert musicians and non-experts to assess six compositions.
The participants weren't told beforehand whether the tunes were composed by humans or computers, but were asked to guess, and then rate how much they liked each one.
items.explain: Q37: The participants *'weren't told beforehand whether the tunes were composed by humans or computers'*. This means they had to assess the music **without knowing** its source. So the correct ending is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: People who thought the composer was a computer tended to dislike the piece more than those who believed it was human.
This was true even among the experts, who might have been expected to be more objective in their analyses.
Where does this prejudice come from?
Paul Bloom of Yale University has a suggestion: he reckons part of the pleasure we get from art stems from the creative process behind the work.
items.explain: Q40: Bloom says pleasure comes from the *'creative process behind the work'*. Kruger says enjoyment increases if people think *'more time and effort was needed'*. Both theories agree that knowing a human made the art adds value — they support, not **cast doubt on**, each other. So the answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: This can give it an 'irresistible essence', says Bloom.
Meanwhile, experiments by Justin Kruger of New York University have shown that people's enjoyment of an artwork increases if they think more time and effort was needed to create it.
items.explain: Q40: Bloom says pleasure comes from the *'creative process behind the work'*. Kruger says enjoyment increases if people think *'more time and effort was needed'*. Both theories agree that knowing a human made the art adds value — they support, not **cast doubt on**, each other. So the answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: Similarly, Colton thinks that when people experience art, they wonder what the artist might have been thinking or what the artist is trying to tell them.
It seems obvious, therefore, that with computers producing art, this speculation is cut short - there's nothing to explore.
But as technology becomes increasingly complex, finding those greater depths in computer art could become possible.
This is precisely why Colton asks the Painting Fool to tap into online social networks for its inspiration: hopefully this way it will choose themes that will already be meaningful to us.

subtitles: Can computers really create works of art?

orphan_explain_map.39: Q39: The passage says non-experts who thought the composer was a computer *'tended to dislike the piece more'*. But it does not say if **all** non-experts responded in the same **predictable way** — some might have liked it. This specific detail is missing, so the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
